title: Formulating Multistage Cutting Stock Problems as QUBO
authors: Marcel Seelbach Benkner, Chiara Capecci, Sebastian Nagies, Javed Akram, Sebastian Rubbert, Dimitrios Bantounas, Philipp Hauke, Michael Johanning, Michael Moeller
abstract: Cutting stock problems are of large relevance to a variety of industry branches. Here, we present a linear programming formulation for a restricted version of the multistage 2D cutting stock problem with Guillotine cuts and test it on published benchmark instances. After this, we derive a non-exact reformulation in quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) form via unbalanced penalization, which we show to have possible benefits in modeling the problem with usable leftovers. This work mainly considers the restricted formulation, in which the dimensions of each cut are determined by those of a single required piece. We further discuss how the approach can be extended to the unrestricted problem, which allows more general cutting patterns involving cuts with dimensions of multiple required pieces and naturally gives rise to quadratic terms in the inequalities of the problem formulation. We showcase solutions via a Simulated Annealing solver for the restricted problem class, where we mainly study the performance of the iterative augmented Lagrangian method. We also discuss possible applications of Quantum Annealing in this setting, as a strong motivation to research QUBO formulations.
summary: This paper tackles the challenging problem of optimizing 2D cutting stock layouts by reformulating it into a QUBO model. By using techniques like unbalanced penalization, they create a quantum-compatible objective function that can be solved on quantum annealers. This work bridges industrial optimization problems with the practical constraints of near-term quantum hardware.
main_problem: The paper focuses on formulating the complex Multistage 2D Cutting Stock Problem (CSP) into a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) format suitable for quantum computation.
main_result: A non-exact QUBO reformulation is derived for the restricted version of the CSP, allowing the incorporation of usable leftover material into the objective function.
method: The approach involves translating the problem from a linear programming formulation into a QUBO form using unbalanced penalization to handle inequality constraints.
model_or_system: The theoretical framework is applied to the 2D CSP, which is then mapped onto the Hamiltonian structure of quantum annealers, referencing trapped-ion architectures like MAGIC.
key_observables: The objective function to be minimized, which relates to minimizing cuts and maximizing usable leftover area ($A_{	ext{rest}}$).
important_parameters: The coupling strengths ($J_{i,j}$) and the penalty coefficients ($\lambda$) used in the QUBO formulation.
main_assumptions: The derived QUBO formulation is non-exact, and the work primarily focuses on the restricted formulation of the CSP.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates different 2D CSP types, contrasting general cuts with simpler Guillotine cuts.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the relevance of CSPs, presents the linear programming model for the restricted case, derives the non-exact QUBO reformulation using penalization, and discusses extensions to the unrestricted problem and potential quantum hardware implementations.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, complex combinatorial optimization problem (CSP) that is successfully mapped onto the QUBO framework, directly motivating and testing the applicability of quantum annealing hardware.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Different types of 2D cutting stock problems. Own visualization based on figure from [15]. Left: a plate of width W and length L is cut into several (here: 5 pieces), where any cuts are allowed. Right: Real-world machines often work with so-called Guillotine cuts, where the plate is cut all the way from one to the other side. These can occur in various stages, where the pieces resulting from a previous stage are further cut into smaller pieces, again using Guillotine cuts.

FIG. 2: Toy example how N = 30 squares of size 200 have to be cut out of a plate to optimize a quadratic energy function depending on an unbalanced penalization parameter λunb.. At λunb. = 0, the cutting plan is not feasible, since the pieces slightly exceed the width of the plate. Note that vertical cuts in the first cutting stage are performed for each column of small squares.

FIG. 3: Results from the augmented Lagrangian method for the gcut 2 and 11 instances from [65]. The left result yields the optimum of the 0-1 integer linear programming formulation, while the right output was still not optimal. Numbers refer to the required pieces.
FIG. 4: QUBOs from the augmented Lagrangian method for the gcut 2 and 11 instances from [65]. Large values in the diagonal are cut off at 10 for better visualization of the off diagonal.
FIG. 5: Solution via 0-1 integer linear programming for the instance okp2 from [66] and for gcut 13 from [65].
